essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to prepare an estimate and quotation for a steel gate and window grilles for a client's house, from the first enquiry to sending the quotation.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would take the client's enquiry and find out what they want: the design, sizes, finish and when they need it. I would visit the site to measure the openings, check the walls and ground for fixing, see the access for delivery and note any hazards. Then I would make or check a drawing and agree it with the client. From the drawing I would do a quantity take-off and cutting list, add a waste allowance, and get prices from suppliers for steel, hardware, paint and any galvanising. I would estimate the labour hours for each task, including cutting, welding, finishing, painting, transport and fixing, and price them at the labour rate. I would add consumables, transport, equipment hire and a share of overheads, then a contingency for risks and the profit mark-up. I would have someone check the figures. Then I would write the quotation with the scope, price, GCT at the current rate, exclusions, validity, payment terms and time to complete, and send it.
markingPoints: Takes the enquiry and visits the site to measure and check conditions
Agrees a drawing; takes off quantities with waste and gets supplier prices
Estimates labour for all tasks, including transport and fixing
Adds consumables, overheads, contingency and profit; figures checked
Quotation with scope, price, GCT, exclusions, validity and terms

essays.stem: Explain the difference between direct costs, overheads, contingency and profit in an estimate. Give a welding workshop example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Direct costs are costs that belong to one job and would not be spent without it. They include the materials, such as the steel, hinges and paint for a gate; the labour hours of the people who make it; consumables such as electrodes, wire, gas and discs; and items such as transport or crane hire for that job. Overheads are the running costs of the business that are shared across all jobs, such as the workshop rent, electricity, insurance, office costs and the owner's admin time. A share of them is added to each job, often as a percentage or an hourly rate. Contingency is an amount added to cover known risks that cannot be priced exactly, such as rotten wall fixings found on site or a steel price rise. Profit is the amount added on top of all costs as the reward for the business, often as a mark-up percentage. Profit is what lets the business grow and buy new equipment.
markingPoints: Direct costs defined with examples
Overheads defined with examples and how they are shared
Contingency defined with an example
Profit defined as added on top of costs
Clear workshop examples throughout

essays.stem: A table frame needs 4 legs of 750 mm, 4 rails of 1200 mm and 4 rails of 600 mm in 40 mm × 40 mm square tube, which comes in 6 m lengths and weighs about 3.3 kg per metre. Work out how many lengths to buy and the mass bought, showing a cutting plan.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the total length needed. Legs: 4 × 0.75 m = 3.0 m. Long rails: 4 × 1.2 m = 4.8 m. Short rails: 4 × 0.6 m = 2.4 m. The total is 3.0 + 4.8 + 2.4 = 10.2 m. One 6 m length is not enough, so at least two are needed. Then I check that the pieces fit into two lengths without joins. Length 1: four 1200 mm rails (4800 mm) and one 750 mm leg = 5550 mm, leaving 450 mm offcut. Length 2: three 750 mm legs (2250 mm) and four 600 mm rails (2400 mm) = 4650 mm, leaving 1350 mm. Both are under 6 m, with room for saw cuts. So I buy 2 lengths, which is 12 m. The mass bought is 12 × 3.3 = 39.6 kg, about 40 kg. The useful offcut of 1350 mm can be kept for another job. I would also check the price per length with the supplier.
markingPoints: Correct total length of 10.2 m
Cutting plan that fits into two 6 m lengths
Allows for saw cuts and notes the offcuts
Correct mass bought: about 39.6 kg
Clear working shown

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the labour time for a fabrication job, and why the welding time alone is not enough.
essays.modelAnswer: I would break the job into tasks: reading the drawing and setting out, marking and cutting, preparing edges, fitting and tacking, welding, cleaning and grinding, inspecting, painting, loading and transport, and fixing on site. For each task I would estimate the time from records of similar past jobs, from standard times the workshop uses, or by working out the quantity and a known rate, such as minutes per metre of weld. I would add time for handling heavy parts, setting up machines, changing over between tasks and cleaning up. Welding time alone is not enough because the arc is only on for part of a welder's day: the rest is spent on handling, fitting, cleaning slag, changing electrodes and inspecting. If only welding time is priced, the job will run at a loss. I would then multiply the hours by the labour rate, check the total against a similar job as a sense check, and after the job compare the real hours with the estimate.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into all its tasks
Uses past records, standard times or rates
Adds handling, set-up and cleaning time
Explains that arc time is only part of the working day
Multiplies by the rate, sense-checks and reviews afterwards

essays.stem: Explain the difference between mark-up and margin, using a worked example, and say why mixing them up is a problem.
essays.modelAnswer: Mark-up is the profit shown as a percentage of the cost. Margin is the profit shown as a percentage of the selling price. For example, a job costs J$80,000. If I add a 25% mark-up, the profit is 25% of J$80,000, which is J$20,000, so the price is J$100,000. The margin on that same job is J$20,000 out of J$100,000, which is 20%. So a 25% mark-up gives only a 20% margin. Mixing them up is a problem because the business may think it is making more profit than it is. If the owner wants a 25% margin but the estimator adds a 25% mark-up, every job will earn less than planned. Over many jobs this can mean the business cannot cover its costs or grow. The estimator should be clear which one the business uses, and check it with a calculation before sending the price.
markingPoints: Mark-up defined as profit on cost
Margin defined as profit on price
Correct worked example
Shows the same profit gives different percentages
Explains the risk of under-pricing if they are confused

essays.stem: Describe the main risks that can make an estimate wrong for a fabrication job in Jamaica, and how an estimator can manage them.
essays.modelAnswer: Material prices can rise between the quote and the purchase, especially for imported steel priced in US dollars when the exchange rate moves. This can be managed with a short validity period, a price-change clause, or buying the steel as soon as the order is confirmed. Site conditions may be different from what was expected, such as weak walls or rock where posts must go, so a site visit and clear exclusions help. The client may change the design, so changes are handled as priced variations agreed in writing. Weather, such as heavy rain or a storm in the hurricane season, can delay site work, so the programme should allow for it. Labour time can be under-estimated, so past records are used and tasks broken down. Errors in sums or quantities are reduced by using a checked spreadsheet and having a second person check. A contingency sum can cover risks that cannot be priced exactly. After the job, the actual costs are compared with the estimate.
markingPoints: Material price and exchange-rate risk, with controls
Site condition risk: site visit and exclusions
Design change risk: written variations
Weather, labour and calculation risks with controls
Contingency and review after the job

essays.stem: Describe what a professional written quotation should contain, and explain why each part matters.
essays.modelAnswer: It should have the business name, address, contact details and the date, and a quotation number so it can be found and referred to. It should name the client and the site. It should describe the scope of the work clearly, with the drawing reference, sizes, materials and finish, so both sides agree on what is included. It should list the exclusions, such as building work or electrical connections, to avoid arguments later. It should give the price, with GCT shown separately at the current rate, so the client knows the full cost. It should say how long the price is valid, because material prices change. It should give the payment terms, such as the deposit and when the balance is due, and the expected time to complete. It may state the warranty. It should have a place for the client to sign to accept it. Clear, neat and accurate quotations make the business look professional and help win work.
markingPoints: Business and client details, date and quotation number
Clear scope with drawing reference and exclusions
Price with GCT shown separately
Validity, payment terms, completion time and warranty
Acceptance signature; explains why each part matters

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the welding consumables for a job: electrodes or wire, shielding gas and grinding discs.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the drawing and list the welds by type and size, then add up the total length of each. For each weld size I would work out the weld metal needed, using a table or the cross-section area times the length, then turn the volume into a mass using the density of steel. Because not all of the electrode or wire ends up in the weld, I would divide by the deposit efficiency: for stick welding much of the electrode is lost as stubs, slag and spatter, while MIG wire is more efficient. That gives the mass of electrodes or wire to buy, rounded up to whole packets or spools. For gas, I would estimate the arc time from the weld length and travel speed, multiply by the flow rate, and compare with the cylinder size. For discs, I would use past jobs to find how many discs are used per metre of weld or per job. I would add a small allowance and check the totals against similar past jobs.
markingPoints: Lists welds and totals their lengths from the drawing
Works out weld metal volume and mass
Allows for deposit efficiency; rounds up to packets or spools
Gas from arc time and flow rate
Discs from past use; sense check with past jobs

essays.stem: Explain why and how the actual costs of a job should be compared with the estimate after the job is finished.
essays.modelAnswer: Comparing actual costs with the estimate shows whether the job made the profit that was planned, and where the estimate was right or wrong. This helps the business price future jobs more accurately and avoid repeating losses. To do it, I would collect the real figures: material invoices and stock used, the labour hours from time sheets, consumables used, subcontract bills, transport and hire costs. I would set them out beside the estimated figures for each cost heading and work out the difference, in J$ and as a percentage. For each large difference, I would find the reason: for example, steel prices rose, a task took longer than expected, there was rework, or the client added work that was not charged. I would write a short review with the lessons learned, such as updating labour rates or adding a step to the checklist, and share it with the estimator and the supervisor. These records then become the past-job data for the next estimate.
markingPoints: Shows whether planned profit was made and improves future estimates
Collects actual figures from invoices and time sheets
Compares heading by heading and calculates differences
Finds reasons for large differences
Records lessons and shares them for future estimates

essays.stem: The client accepted your quotation for a gate, and now asks for a matching pedestrian gate and a different paint colour. Describe how you would handle this.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank the client and make sure I understand exactly what they want: the size and design of the pedestrian gate and the new colour. I would explain that these are changes to the agreed job, called variations, and that I will price them before doing the work. I would measure for the pedestrian gate, then estimate its materials, labour, hardware, finishing and fixing in the same way as the main job. For the colour, I would check whether it costs more, for example a special paint or a different coating, and whether it delays the job. I would send a written variation quotation with the extra price, GCT at the current rate, any change to the completion date and the payment terms, and ask the client to sign to accept it. I would not start the extra work until it is approved. I would update the job plan, order the extra materials and tell the team. All of this would be kept on the job file.
markingPoints: Clarifies exactly what the client wants
Explains they are variations to be priced
Estimates the extra work properly, including any time impact
Written variation quotation, signed approval before starting
Updates the plan, orders materials, informs the team, keeps records

practical1.title: Measure an opening and take off quantities for a security grille or gate
practical1.brief: As a team, measure a real door or window opening at the Centre that the assessor shows you, and estimate the materials for a steel security grille or gate to fit it. First, agree who measures, who sketches, who checks and who writes up. Measure the opening at the top, middle and bottom for width and at each side for height, check it for square with the diagonals, and note the wall type and any obstacles. Draw a dimensioned sketch of the grille or gate to the design the assessor gives you, with the sizes of the frame, bars and fixings. From your sketch, write a cutting list (each piece, length and number) and a material take-off: the section sizes, the total length of each section, the number of stock lengths to buy (use the stock length the assessor gives), the mass from the section table, the hardware, paint and fixings. Each member measures at least one dimension and checks one calculation done by another member. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the sketch, cutting list and take-off are finished.
materials: Tape measures, steel rule, square and spirit level
Design brief and steel section table (mass per metre) from the assessor
Squared paper, pencils, eraser and calculator
Cutting list and material take-off forms
photos: The team measuring the opening, with the tape in place
The site notes with all the measurements and diagonals
The dimensioned sketch of the grille or gate
The material take-off with stock lengths and mass
A member checking another member's calculation
checklist: Measured accurately at several points and checked for square
Recorded site conditions that affect the job (wall type, obstacles)
Helped draw a clear, dimensioned sketch
Wrote correct cut lengths and numbers on the cutting list
Worked out stock lengths and mass correctly, with waste allowed
Checked another member's calculation and corrected errors
Worked well with the team and kept the measuring area safe
safety: Use a safe step or platform, not a chair, to reach high measurements
Keep doorways and walkways clear while measuring
Retract steel tapes slowly; their edges can cut
Follow the Centre's rules for working in occupied rooms

practical2.title: Price a fabrication job, write the quotation and present it to a client (role play)
practical2.brief: As a team, price the grille or gate from Practical 1 (or a job the assessor gives you) and present the quotation. The assessor gives you a supplier price list, the labour rate, the overhead rate, the mark-up and the GCT rate to use. First, agree roles: materials, labour, consumables and other costs, checking, and writing the quotation. Price the materials from your take-off. Break the labour into tasks (cutting, fitting, welding, finishing, painting, transport, fixing) and estimate the hours for each. Add consumables, transport, overheads and a contingency, then the mark-up, then GCT. Set it out on an estimate sheet (a spreadsheet may be used). Have a team member who did not do a part check its figures. Write a professional quotation. Then role-play a client meeting: one member plays the client, two present the quotation, and the client asks for a variation from the assessor's card, which you price and confirm in writing. Swap roles so that every member presents or answers at least once. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the estimate, the quotation and the variation note are finished.
materials: Take-off from Practical 1, or a job brief from the assessor
Supplier price list, labour rate, overhead rate, mark-up and GCT rate from the assessor
Estimate sheet and quotation form (paper or a spreadsheet on a computer)
Client role card and variation card from the assessor
photos: The materials priced on the estimate sheet
The labour broken into tasks with hours
The completed estimate showing overheads, contingency, mark-up and GCT
A member checking another member's figures
The client role play in progress
The written variation with the client's signature
checklist: Priced materials correctly from the take-off
Broke labour into tasks with sensible hours
Included consumables, transport, overheads and contingency
Applied the mark-up and GCT correctly and showed GCT separately
Checked another member's figures and corrected errors
Helped write a clear, complete and professional quotation
Presented or answered the client politely and accurately
Priced the variation and confirmed it in writing
safety: Sit comfortably at the computer with the screen at eye level; take short breaks
Keep cables tidy so no one trips
Keep role play respectful and professional
